Bluespotted cornetfish Fistularia commersonii is a widespread Indo-Pacific species that attains a notable ultimate total length of 160 centimeters [Li = 160 centimeters], making it one of the larger members of the Fistulariidae family. Individuals held under controlled conditions at 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C] exhibited a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 5% [GSI = 5%]. The relationship between body size and reproductive readiness is further reflected in the length at which 50 percent of individuals attain sexual maturity, known as the total length at puberty, which has been estimated at 65 centimeters [Lp = 65 centimeters]. This length threshold is reached after a substantial period of juvenile growth, during which the fish must acquire sufficient size to handle the large-bodied prey typical of its diet.

The early life stages of Fistularia commersonii are characterised by a short embryonic period when water temperatures are favourable. In laboratory rearing trials conducted at 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C], the age at birth, defined as the time from fertilisation to eclosion, was recorded at approximately 10 days [ab = approximately 10 days], a developmental pace comparable to that of other tropical teleosts with pelagic eggs. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva is minute, weighing only 0.0014 grams [Wwb = 0.0014 grams] at the moment of chorion rupture. This extremely low wet weight at birth reflects the small egg diameter of roughly 1.5 millimeters and the limited yolk reserves available to the endotrophic larva before it must initiate first exogenous feeding. Following hatching, the prolarva undergoes a brief yolk absorption stage, during which its mouth gapes open and retinal differentiation proceeds, enabling the first prey capture events that mark the transition to exotrophic nutrition. The rapidity of this early ontogenetic trajectory is typical of warm-water marine fish larvae that face high predation pressure in the planktonic environment.

As juveniles transition into the sub-adult phase, somatic growth proceeds steadily until individuals approach the size at which reproductive maturation begins. The wet weight at puberty, based on length-weight regressions derived from field-collected specimens, reaches approximately 5300 grams [Wwi = approximately 5300 grams], a substantial body mass that highlights the considerable energetic investment required before gametogenesis can commence. In contrast, the ultimate wet weight, representing the maximum adult body mass attained by fully grown individuals, is considerably lower at 354 grams [Wwp = 354 grams]. This apparent discrepancy arises because the ultimate wet weight is calculated from the length-weight relationship at the ultimate total length, whereas the wet weight at puberty reflects the mass of a fish that has already achieved a size capable of supporting reproductive activity. The species thus exhibits a life-history pattern in which individuals reach a moderate adult mass but require a much larger body size, and consequently a longer growing period, to initiate reproduction, a trait that may buffer against recruitment variability in variable reef environments.

Longevity records for Bluespotted cornetfish remain limited, but captive observations provide useful insights into the species' potential lifespan. A single individual maintained under laboratory conditions survived for approximately 3.5 years, which, when converted to a standard chronological measure, corresponds to a lifespan of about 1825 days [am = about 1825 days] at a holding temperature of 17.2 °C [T = 17.2 °C]. This relatively modest maximum lifespan, compared to other reef-associated piscivores, may be linked to the species' rapid early growth and early reproductive maturity, which are typical of an opportunistic life-history strategy in a thermally stable environment. Field-based estimates of longevity in wild populations remain tentative, but the available laboratory data suggest that individuals rarely exceed four years of age under natural conditions, where predation and foraging constraints likely impose additional mortality pressures. The thermal dependence of metabolic rates in this species implies that lifespan could vary across its broad geographic range, with cooler-water populations potentially experiencing slower senescence.

Reproductive output in Fistularia commersonii has been characterised through the analysis of gonadal tissue from mature females. Fecundity per reproductive event is estimated at approximately 5000 eggs per spawning [N_R_i = approximately 5000 eggs per spawning], with spawning frequency being variable but thought to occur at a rate of approximately 2 events per month [F_R_i = approximately 2 events per month] during peak reproductive months. This iteroparous strategy, combined with the production of small, buoyant eggs that develop rapidly, allows the species to exploit transient pulses of planktonic productivity.
